content: The studies conducted in 2014 were carried out across various countries, including Brazil, Canada, Greece, India (two trials), Italy, Rwanda, South Africa, Switzerland, Thailand (two trials), and the United States of America (nine trials). Three of these trials involved more than two arms and contributed to two separate comparisons. One trial exclusively included women undergoing elective cesarean sections (122 women), while seven trials focused solely on non-elective cesarean sections (2922 women). Five trials included both elective and non-elective cesarean sections (1635 women), and seven trials did not specify the type of cesarean section (1254 women). All trials utilized parenteral administration of antibiotics. Eleven trials (3808 women) administered a single intravenous (IV) dose to women in both groups, while four trials (803 women) administered multiple IV doses to both groups. One trial (400 women) compared a single IV dose of first-generation cephalosporin with multiple intramuscular doses of natural penicillins. Four trials (922 women) did not describe the route of administration; three of these trials used multiple doses, and one used a single dose in both groups. Sixteen trials administered antibiotics at or immediately after cord clamping (5217 women). Two trials administered antibiotics preoperatively: one trial administered them up to 60 minutes before the incision (132 women), and the other administered them immediately before the incision (59 women). Two trials did not specify the timing of antibiotic administration (525 women). The Cochrane review did not include priority outcomes such as antimicrobial resistance, maternal well-being, maternal satisfaction, and neonatal mortality. Additionally, maternal death, cost of care, and neonatal infection were not reported in any of the included studies. Subgroup analyses by type of cesarean section were limited. For outcomes such as maternal sepsis and endometritis, the number of studies was small, and few studies defined the type of cesarean section, making the subgroup analysis results less meaningful. Regarding the effects of anti-staphylococcal cephalosporins (first and second generation) versus broad-spectrum penicillins plus beta-lactamase inhibitors, the evidence was of very low certainty. It remains unclear whether anti-staphylococcal cephalosporins reduce maternal sepsis, wound infection rates, or maternal composite adverse effects compared to broad-spectrum penicillins plus beta-lactamase inhibitors. For minimally anti-staphylococcal cephalosporins (third generation) versus broad-spectrum penicillins plus beta-lactamase inhibitors, the evidence was also of very low certainty. It is unclear whether third-generation cephalosporins reduce severe infectious morbidity, puerperal infection, wound infection, or maternal composite adverse effects compared to broad-spectrum penicillins plus beta-lactamase inhibitors. The Cochrane review authors noted substantial statistical heterogeneity in the results for endometritis, maternal fever, and maternal urinary tract infection. This heterogeneity appeared to be explained by one small outlying study, which was the only study to administer antibiotics before skin incision rather than at or after cord clamping. Further investigation is required to confirm whether the timing of antibiotic administration is an important explanatory factor. A systematic review of qualitative studies on women’s perspectives and experiences with antibiotics for preventing infection at birth identified one study involving 21 women in the United Kingdom. Women described their recovery from cesarean sections as being influenced by pain, limited mobility, caregiving challenges, and concerns about wound infection or non-healing. Many women reported receiving inadequate information about the risks of postoperative infections, including endometritis, or the potential for prevention through vaginal cleansing. A 2018 systematic review of qualitative studies on women’s preferences for intrapartum care found that most women desire a positive birth experience with good outcomes for both mother and baby, while acknowledging that medical intervention may sometimes be necessary. Women, particularly first-time mothers, often feel apprehensive about labor and birth and are wary of medical interventions, though they may welcome interventions in certain contexts to address recognized complications. Women prefer to receive relevant information from technically competent healthcare providers who are sensitive to their needs. A 2018 core outcome set for maternal infectious morbidity outcomes in cesarean delivery was proposed based on a systematic review of 452 trials and a Delphi survey of 40 review authors. The proposed core outcomes included endometritis (primary outcome), maternal mortality, wound infection, wound complications, febrile morbidity, and neonatal morbidity. Two out of 46 trials included in the Cochrane review reported cost outcomes. One study compared the effectiveness of ceftriaxone versus a triple-drug regimen (metronidazole, ampicillin, and cloxacillin plus gentamicin) for preventing cesarean section infections. The study, conducted in two tertiary hospitals in Nigeria, reported a mean cost difference of $9 for ceftriaxone versus $15 for the triple regimen, with no difference in hospital stay duration or maternal outcomes. The authors concluded that the cheaper single-dose antibiotic was as effective as the more expensive triple regimen. Another single-center study in the USA reported the cost of prophylactic antibiotics to prevent post-cesarean infections as $5026 (in 1986), based on daily hospital charges, laboratory tests, drug costs, and other factors. However, this study was assessed as low quality. The main resource requirements for administering intravenous antibiotics include skilled healthcare professionals, training on safe injection practices, and appropriate equipment and infrastructure.
